title: Ecotourism

definition.text: Travel to natural places that aims to do little harm and to support conservation and environmental education.

facts.text: Some definitions also require that it pays its way for the host community or makes conservation financially possible.
It is treated as one part of the wider field of sustainable tourism, and it differs from plain nature tourism by aiming to build tourists' appreciation of habitats and local culture.
Its possible benefits include visitor spending and jobs, money to run and expand protected areas, and a reason to protect or restore natural land.
In South Africa, 70% of the money national parks make comes straight from tourism.
Visitors can still damage protected areas, raise local rents and property values, and bring health risks to people and wildlife.
Most ecotourism businesses are owned by foreign investors, so most profits leave the area instead of going back into the local economy or conservation.
Like most long-distance travel, it often depends on flying, which adds to climate change, and few operators have a net-positive effect on the environment.
Weak regulation lets damaging operations such as underwater hotels and helicopter tours call themselves ecotourism, a form of greenwashing.

contested_note: Environmentalists, interest groups and governments define ecotourism differently, and where tourism stops being ecotourism is disputed.

definition.text: The rules and measures used to stop ecotourism operations from damaging the places they sell, from visitor limits to certification labels.

facts.text: They include setting a carrying capacity, hardening sites, sustainable design, visitor quotas, fees, access limits and visitor education.
Labels such as the European Ecotourism Labelling Standard try to certify genuine low-impact operators.
When responsible operators are not recognised, they are put at a competitive disadvantage against greenwashed ones.

title: Underdevelopment tourism
article: Ecotourism#Small scale, slow growth, and local control

definition.text: The idea that multinational companies control ecotourism development and take most of its gains, leaving local communities without ownership.

facts.text: It can limit local control over natural resources and raises questions about the unequal sharing of tourism's benefits.
Large corporate ecotourism projects can cause heavy environmental damage, loss of traditional culture and exploitation of local workers.

definition.text: The branch of philosophy that studies natural things for their beauty and other aesthetic qualities.

facts.text: Its main ideas, including disinterestedness, the picturesque and positive aesthetics, were developed in the 18th and 19th centuries.
Disinterestedness means judging something aesthetically while setting aside personal and practical interests.

Andrew Lothian's The Science of Scenery (2017) measured scenic beauty by asking the public to rate landscape photographs, a method critics said favours the picturesque and ignores bodily experience of places.
Aldo Leopold named integrity, stability and beauty as the three features of ecosystems that give rise to a land ethic.
Fractal patterns that echo nature can make human-built spaces more visually soothing, and people prefer particular levels of fractal complexity.
Environmental aesthetics is one branch of environmental philosophy, next to environmental ethics.

definition.text: Three classic ways of appreciating nature: the tame beauty of gardens, the awe of wild and threatening nature, and nature seen as picture-like scenes.

facts.text: Beautiful things tend to be small, smooth and fair in colour, while sublime things tend to be powerful, intense and terrifying.
The picturesque mixes the two: varied, irregular, rich and forceful.
Viewed with disinterest, the frightening side of nature, such as mountains and wilderness, can be admired rather than feared.

definition.text: How far a person counts nature as part of who they are.

facts.text: It behaves like a personality trait, staying fairly stable over time and across situations, yet it can grow after time spent in nature.
Schultz split it into three parts: feeling at one with nature (cognitive), caring for nature (affective) and committing to protect it (behavioural).
People who feel highly connected to nature report higher psychological and social well-being.
It reliably predicts environmental behaviour: highly connected people are more likely to join environmental groups and call themselves environmentalists.
A meta-analysis confirmed its strong correlation with pro-environmental behaviour but found a weaker causal role than the correlations suggested.
Raising people's connection to nature may motivate ecological behaviour more effectively than laws and rules.
More nature exposure and easier access to city green space may raise well-being and ecological behaviour, which matters to planners.

definition.text: A 21-item questionnaire that measures how connected to nature a person feels as a lasting trait.

facts.text: At least seventeen scales measure nature connectedness; the most used are Nature Relatedness, Nature Connectedness and Inclusion of Nature in Self.
Its three subscales measure identifying with nature, concern about human effects on the environment, and comfort and wish to be in nature.
It shows good reliability, alpha = .87, and test-retest stability six months later, alpha = .85.

definition.text: The probable fall in people's direct contact with nature, which earlier studies link to effects on health and on care for the environment.

facts.text: One review concluded that within a generation children's lives have largely moved indoors, while childhood nature experience builds lifelong care for nature.
A global review found the evidence still too thin to judge how large or general the decline is.
Indoor lifestyles and growing screen time have cut human contact with nature.

title: Nature therapy

definition.text: A broad group of treatments, also called ecotherapy, that use time in nature to improve mental or physical health.

facts.text: Its forms include forest therapy, forest bathing (shinrin-yoku) and Sami Lok.
Japan's forestry ministry head Tomohide Akiyama popularised forest bathing in 1982 to get more people into forests.
Its effects are usually tied to the body's stress recovery, as contact with nature lowers cortisol and heart rate.
Qing Li's small trials from 2005 found that walking in a forest for a few hours a day raised natural killer cells by roughly 50 percent; urban walks had no such effect.
Contact with nature is associated with lower stress and fewer depressive symptoms.
It is cheap and accessible, needing only parks, community gardens or other public outdoor space.
Reviews find results vary with study design, many studies rely on self-reports, and the evidence is not yet enough for clinical guidelines or proof of cause.

contested_note: Reviews disagree on how strong the evidence is, with some calling results inconclusive and asking for larger randomized trials.

definition.text: Health-system programmes in which doctors or public agencies formally send people to spend time in nature.

facts.text: Canada lets physicians formally prescribe nature, and since 2019 UK general practitioners have referred patients to the NHS-funded Dose of Nature programme.
Dose of Nature claimed a 64% recovery rate for its first 1500 patients, against 50% for talk therapy.
Finnish researchers recommend about five hours a month in nature as preventive health care.

definition.text: The idea that humans have an inborn urge to seek connection with nature and other living things.

facts.text: Edward O. Wilson introduced and popularised it in his 1984 book Biophilia; Erich Fromm had first used the word.
It has been developed within evolutionary psychology: ancestors with closer ties to nature may have found food, water and shelter more easily.
Research suggests modern cities are poorly suited to minds that evolved in natural settings.
It is used to explain why people keep plants, care for animals and sometimes risk their lives to save them.
Conservationists worry that losing this connection could breed disregard for wild species and speed ecosystem loss, so reconnecting people with nature has become a conservation goal.
It inspires biophilic cities with more green space, which can also serve as wildlife corridors.
Fromm treated biophilia as a biologically normal instinct, and the term has since spread to many fields of study.
Its opposite, biophobia, is an inherited fear of nature and animals, such as fear of snakes and spiders.

definition.text: A neuroscience model holding that human vision has adapted to process nature's fractal patterns, those that repeat at different scales, with ease.

facts.text: Clouds, mountains and trees are natural fractals.
People process fractals with a fractal dimension between 1.3 and 1.5 especially well, and viewing them lowers physiological stress and boosts thinking.
Designers add biophilic fractals to buildings because people spend 92% of their time indoors.

title: Indigenous kinship with nature
article: Biophilia hypothesis#Indigenous perspectives on the human-nature connection

definition.text: The view, common in many Indigenous cultures, that humans are part of the natural world and bound to it by kinship and reciprocity.

facts.text: Humans, animals, plants and soil are seen as depending on each other for survival and health.
It underlies traditional ecological knowledge, such as the controlled burns used by some Native American and Aboriginal Australian societies.
Indigenous and animist beliefs usually treat nature as sacred, and the Anishinaabe make offerings before harvesting wild rice.

title: Attention restoration theory

definition.text: The theory that time in nature, or even views of it, helps people recover from the mental tiredness caused by sustained deliberate focus.

facts.text: Stephen and Rachel Kaplan argued that busy modern settings tax directed attention, which can run down into attention fatigue.
Nature evokes soft fascination, effortless attention to gentle stimuli such as drifting clouds or flowing water, which lets the mind rest.
A restorative setting has four properties: being away, extent, compatibility and fascination.
It builds on William James's distinction between effortful voluntary attention and automatic involuntary attention.
Roger Ulrich's competing Stress Reduction Theory says nature's benefits come from emotional and physiological responses rather than cognitive ones.

notes: Crawled page with no dossier block of its own; drafted here because the chapter's Restoration material depends on it.

definition.text: Leisure activity done for enjoyment, amusement or pleasure.

facts.text: The need to do something for recreation is treated as a basic part of human biology and psychology.
It needs leisure: time free from work, sleep, daily chores and social duties.
Affluence, population trends and the growing commercial supply of recreation have raised its role in modern life.
Parks and beaches are key venues, and tourism has recognised that many visitors come specifically for recreation.
Recreation and tourism are among the cultural services ecosystems provide, alongside spiritual fulfilment.
When biodiversity is lost, ecosystems can no longer offer the same areas for recreation and tourism.
Leisure is a human right under the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

definition.text: A profession that uses recreation's health benefits as a form of therapy.

facts.text: It is used in rehabilitation, youth and adult psychiatric care, and the care of elderly, disabled and chronically ill people.
In the United States, practitioners certified by the NCTRC are called Certified Therapeutic Recreation Specialists.

title: Sense of place

definition.text: The many-sided relationship between people and places, covering what makes a place special and the attachment people feel to it.

facts.text: Some treat it as a quality certain places have; others treat it as a feeling held by people rather than the place.
It need not be positive: geographer Yi-Fu Tuan pointed to senses of place such as fear.
Places with a strong sense of place have an identity deeply felt by residents and visitors, and designations such as World Heritage Sites try to protect them.
Childhood places form a primal landscape that becomes part of identity and a baseline for judging places later in life.
Climate-driven damage to valued places can bring grief and solastalgia, and many Indigenous cultures are losing their sense of place to climate change.
Contact with natural environments strengthens social ties, stewardship and sense of place.

notes: S:3c4029a53b87 (Nature therapy) carries an [unreliable medical source?] tag.

definition.text: The quality of places that lack a sense of place and feel as if they could be anywhere.

facts.text: Cultural geographer Edward Relph studied placelessness, and anthropologist Marc Augé called such locations non-places.
Strip malls, petrol stations, fast food chains and chain stores are cited examples.
Historic districts heavily commercialised for tourism can lose their sense of place.

definition.text: A landscape shaped by the long interplay of human activity and the natural environment.

facts.text: The World Heritage Committee sorts them into three kinds: landscapes designed by people, organically evolved landscapes (relict or continuing), and associative landscapes valued for religious, artistic or cultural ties.
Geographer Otto Schlüter first used the term academically in the early 20th century, contrasting original landscape with landscape made by culture.
Carl O. Sauer's classic definition: culture is the agent, the natural area is the medium, and the cultural landscape is the result.
In 1992 the World Heritage Committee began revising its guidelines so properties neither purely natural nor purely cultural could be listed as cultural landscapes.
Tongariro National Park in New Zealand became the first property listed under these criteria in 1993; its mountains hold spiritual meaning for the Maori.
The concept helps conserve heritage by linking buildings, local materials and traditions into one idea of identity and place, and by shifting focus to managing future change.
The Dresden Elbe Valley was removed from the World Heritage list in 2009 after a four-lane highway was built across the Elbe.

definition.text: The link between spending time in natural surroundings and a person's mental health.

facts.text: Studies count almost any contact with nature as exposure, from a hike or a forest visit to a walk in a park or time by a lake.
Contact with nature is tied to lower stress, better mood, more happiness and meaning, and less mental distress.
An eighteen-year Danish study found children raised with the most green space had 55% less risk of developing several psychiatric disorders.
A 10-year UK study found that greener surroundings within 300m of home and nearby green and blue spaces both lowered the risk of anxiety and depression.
Nature exposure improves working memory, attention and cognitive flexibility, while urban settings have been linked to attention deficits.
Even short exposure helps: students who glimpsed a flowering green roof for 40 seconds made fewer errors on a dull task than those shown a concrete roof.
Modern indoor, screen-heavy lifestyles have reduced people's contact with nature.
Therapists use nature in treatments called ecotherapy.

title: City parks and mental health
article: Nature exposure and mental health#City parks and mental health

definition.text: The benefit that parks inside cities bring to the mental health of the people living near them.

facts.text: Residents living 800m to 1.6km from a park had mental health scores 4.5 points lower than residents within 400m of one.
Urban parks help reduce stress and lower the risk of anxiety and depression.
Being cheap and open to all, urban parks can make mental health benefits accessible regardless of income or background.

definition.text: Travel to enjoy an area's natural attractions, including its plants and animals.

facts.text: It overlaps with wildlife and adventure tourism and includes ecotourism, which focuses on environmental education and conservation.
Variants include stargazing, cycling and birdwatching tourism.
National parks have become closely associated with it.
It can harm the environment, but it can also aid conservation by making remaining natural areas more valuable to local people and landowners.

definition.text: Leisure activity done outdoors, usually in natural settings.

facts.text: Activities range from fishing, hunting and walking to hiking, camping, climbing, kayaking and skiing.
People pursue it for exercise, general wellbeing and spiritual renewal, with less stress on competition than organised sport.
It often takes place in thinly populated areas with mountains, lakes, rivers and scenic views.
In 2024 outdoor recreation accounted for $696.7 billion of value added, 2.4 percent of US GDP, according to the US Bureau of Economic Analysis.
University outdoor programs have been shown to help students' wellbeing and stress levels.
Forest managers count outdoor recreation among the objectives forests serve, alongside timber, conservation and hunting.

definition.text: A natural feature or area of land or water that holds special spiritual meaning for a people or community.

facts.text: They include mountains, forests, groves, trees, rivers, lakes, caves, islands and springs, ranging from a single tree to whole mountain ranges.
They exist on every continent except Antarctica; India alone has at least 13,720 reported sacred groves, with an estimated 100,000 to 150,000 in total.
Many have been protected for long periods with little use, and some are notably rich in biodiversity.
Besides sheltering species, they can supply water, medicines and other ecosystem services and support pilgrimage and tourism.
Some have been governed by taboos excluding women or marginalised groups, so they should not be romanticised.
The Convention on Biological Diversity recognised an urgent need to protect them and in 2004 issued the Akwe Kon guidelines for assessing developments that may affect them.

definition.text: Well-being, or happiness, as judged by the people whose lives are being assessed rather than from an outside, objective view.

facts.text: Ed Diener defined it by three signs: frequent positive feelings, infrequent negative feelings, and judgments such as life satisfaction.
Its three components are affect (emotions and moods), life satisfaction (judgments about one's life) and eudaimonia (a sense of meaning and purpose).
It is usually measured by self-report, often with questionnaires on life satisfaction, the most common measure in the field.
Its definitions usually leave out objective conditions such as material wealth or health, although these can influence ratings.
Top-down theories trace it to stable personality, while bottom-up theories see happiness built from happy experiences and fulfilled basic needs.
Quality of social connections affects it much more strongly than their number.
Nature relatedness, a person's felt connection with nature, has been found to directly affect it, raising affect and life satisfaction.
Happiness economics often uses it to appraise the wellbeing of whole populations.

definition.text: The idea that each person has an inherited baseline level of subjective well-being to which they tend to return.

facts.text: Top-down theories hold that people have a genetic tendency to be happy or unhappy that fixes their well-being setpoint.
Personality studies find genetics account for 20–48% of the variance in Five-Factor traits, and the variance in subjective well-being is also heritable.

title: Sustainable tourism

definition.text: Tourism that attends to its economic, social and environmental effects while improving visitors' experiences and meeting the needs of host communities.

facts.text: It grew out of sustainable development, and the term is open to varied interpretations.
As tourism is one of the world's largest and fastest-growing industries, its growth will put heavy stress on remaining biodiverse habitats and Indigenous cultures.
Local communities can gain jobs, economic development and infrastructure from it.
Carrying capacity is a key consideration in ecologically sensitive or remote areas.
Tourism's dependence on fossil fuels ties sustainable tourism closely to sustainable transport and climate change.
The Global Sustainable Tourism Council's GSTC Criteria serve as the international standard for certifying sustainable tourism businesses.
Critics call it an oxymoron because tourism is extractive and cannot continue indefinitely.
The movement emerged after the environmental awareness of the 1960s and 1970s amid growing mass tourism.

contested_note: Critics argue that tourism is inherently extractive, so 'sustainable tourism' is a contradiction in terms.

definition.text: The behaviours and practices of travellers and providers that can lead to sustainable tourism.

facts.text: It aims to maximise benefits to local communities and minimise negative social or environmental impacts.
Both service providers and consumers are held accountable for the tourism they develop or take part in.
Some critics argue it distracts from wider issues needing regulation, such as visitor numbers and environmental impact.

definition.text: Tourism that aims not just to leave no trace but to leave positive benefits for the natural world.

facts.text: It is a form of regenerative tourism meant to help reverse declines in nature by 2030 and achieve full recovery by 2050.
The World Travel and Tourism Council says 80% of goods and services in the industry are highly dependent on nature.
Actions include supporting reforestation, making space for nature in urban hotels, and cutting light and water pollution.

title: Tourism carrying capacity

definition.text: The largest number of visitors a destination can take at once without damaging its environment, economy or community or spoiling the visitor experience.

facts.text: The idea came from range, habitat and wildlife management, where managers sought the largest population a habitat could support over a long time.
Even an imperfect estimate can guide visitor caps; Peru limits Inca Trail hikers to 500 per day because geologists warned more could cause serious erosion.
Physical capacity is how many people fit on a site, usually assumed at around 1m per person.
Social capacity is exceeded when local tolerance falls, visitor enjoyment drops and crime rises; biophysical capacity is passed when damage outruns a habitat's ability to regenerate.
Economic capacity can mark the point where tourism revenue is overtaken by the inflation tourism causes.
How much damage is acceptable is a matter of human judgment; where pristine conditions are the goal, carrying capacity may be zero.
Critics say it wrongly assumes stable social-ecological systems and is hard to calculate, and UNESCO warns it can make a site look better protected than it is.

contested_note: Several authors argue the concept is flawed both in its assumptions and in practice, and it has largely been replaced by management-by-objectives frameworks.

title: Limits of acceptable change
article: Tourism carrying capacity#Limits of acceptable change

definition.text: A visitor-management framework that monitors a site against set objectives instead of relying on a single maximum visitor number.

facts.text: The US Forest Service developed it in the 1980s as the first framework to follow carrying capacity.
It assumes any tourist activity has some impact, so a visitor cap is only one tool among many.
It is often summarised as a nine-step process, from selecting indicators of resource and social conditions to choosing preferred management alternatives.

definition.text: What is good for a person in itself: a measure of how well their life is going for them.

facts.text: It is also called welfare or quality of life.
Broadly it covers the balance of all good and bad aspects of a life; narrowly it means only the good, in contrast to ill-being.
Money and medicine can contribute to well-being as causes but are not themselves forms of it.
There is wide agreement that positive emotions, achievements, relationships and health usually contribute to it.
It can be assessed for an individual or for a whole community, whose well-being includes economic, social, environmental and cultural aspects.
Welfare economics studies how economic activity affects it, using metrics such as income distribution, GDP and consumer surplus to compare policies.
Defenders of anthropocentrism argue a healthy environment is needed for human well-being rather than for its own sake.
Its study began in antiquity as discussions of how to live a good life.

definition.text: The main philosophical accounts of what well-being consists of: hedonism, desire theories and objective list theories.

facts.text: Hedonism holds that pleasure and pain are the only factors of well-being.
Desire theories hold that people fare well when they get what they want.
Objective list theories add items such as health, friendship, achievement, knowledge and autonomy that benefit a person whether or not they care about them.
Jeremy Bentham, father of classical utilitarianism, proposed the felicific calculus to measure and add up pleasure and pain.

title: Stress recovery theory

definition.text: The idea that contact with nature helps the body and emotions recover from stress, lowering cortisol and heart rate.

facts.text: It is usually discussed alongside attention restoration theory; the two describe complementary ways nature may benefit wellbeing.
The benefits of nature therapy are usually linked to this stress recovery process.
Urban forestry has been shown to promote stress recovery and psychological healing.

notes: Phrase concept; the source calls it Stress Reduction Theory (SRT).
